before:
• Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 provides that causes of action for injuries to a person survive the death of either party. Your claim can be brought against the deceased driver's estate.
  • South Carolina: S.C. Code § 15-5-90 similarly allows personal injury claims to survive the death of the tortfeasor (the person who caused the harm).

In practical terms, this means your claim proceeds in one of three ways: through the deceased driver's liability insurance, through a lawsuit against their estate, or through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.
after:
• Georgia: O.C.G.A. § 9-2-41 provides that causes of action for injuries to a person survive the death of either party. Your claim is brought against the driver's personal representative (executor or administrator), though no punitive damages are allowed against the personal representative.
  • South Carolina: S.C. Code § 15-5-90 similarly allows personal injury claims to survive the death of the tortfeasor (the person who caused the harm).

In practical terms, this means your claim proceeds in one of three ways: through the deceased driver's liability insurance, through a lawsuit against their estate's personal representative, or through your own uninsured/underinsured motorist coverage.

before: When you sue an estate, you are not suing the deceased person's family members personally. You are suing the legal entity that represents the deceased person's assets and liabilities. The estate is managed by a personal representative (also called an executor or administrator) who is appointed by the probate court.
after: When you sue an estate, you are not suing the deceased person's family members personally. You are suing the estate's personal representative (also called an executor or administrator), appointed by the probate court, in that capacity.

before:
• The lawsuit names the estate as the defendant — for example, "Estate of John Smith, Deceased"
  • The personal representative defends the case on behalf of the estate
  • The deceased driver's liability insurance typically still provides the defense and pays any judgment up to policy limits
  • If the judgment exceeds policy limits, the estate's assets (bank accounts, property, investments) may be used to satisfy the remainder
  • Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk unless they co-signed the driver's insurance policy or were otherwise independently liable
after:
• The lawsuit names the personal representative, in that capacity, as the defendant — for example, "Jane Smith, as Administrator of the Estate of John Smith"; in Georgia an estate is not a legal entity that can be sued (Orange County Trust Co. v. Estate of Takowsky, 1969)
  • The personal representative defends the case on behalf of the estate
  • The deceased driver's liability insurance typically still provides the defense and pays any judgment up to policy limits
  • If the judgment exceeds policy limits, the estate's assets (bank accounts, property, investments) may be used to satisfy the remainder
  • Family members' personal assets are generally not at risk unless they owned or furnished the vehicle for family use (the family purpose doctrine) or were otherwise independently negligent

before: Under Georgia law, creditors (including personal injury claimants) must file their claims with the estate within a specific timeframe. Georgia requires creditors to file within the later of: (1) three months after the personal representative publishes notice to creditors, or (2) the general statute of limitations for the underlying claim.
after: Under Georgia law, the personal representative must publish a notice to creditors (including personal injury claimants) within 60 days of qualifying. Written notice of your claim within three months of the last published notice preserves your equal share in distributions, but missing it does not bar the claim (O.C.G.A. § 53-7-41). No suit may be filed against the personal representative until six months after qualification (O.C.G.A. § 53-7-42), and the two-year limitation period is tolled, up to five years, while the estate has no personal representative (O.C.G.A. § 9-3-93).

before: South Carolina's probate process is similar. The probate court appoints a personal representative, and creditors must file claims against the estate. South Carolina requires that claims be filed within one year from the date of the decedent's death or within the applicable statute of limitations, whichever is earlier.
after: South Carolina's probate process is similar. The probate court appoints a personal representative, and creditors must present claims against the estate. To reach the estate's own assets, a claim must be presented within the earlier of one year after the death or eight months after the first published notice to creditors (sixty days after any written notice) (S.C. Code §§ 62-3-801 and 62-3-803(a)). That bar does not apply, up to the policy limits, to a claim covered by the driver's liability insurance (S.C. Code § 62-3-803(d)(2)), and the three-year limitation period is suspended for eight months after the death (S.C. Code § 62-3-802(b)).

The interaction between the personal injury statute of limitations and the probate creditor deadline can create a compressed timeline. If the at-fault driver died in the accident, you may need to act quickly to ensure your claim is filed properly in both the civil court and the probate proceeding. Do not assume you have the full two or three years — consult an attorney as soon as possible.
